- **Owning chapter:** C18

<a id="gl-tradeoff"></a>

### tradeoff

- **Definition:** A choice in which gaining on one dimension costs something on another, stated with what is given up.
- **Example:** Shipping two weeks sooner by cutting the search filters from the first release.
- **Non-example:** Calling one option "best" without naming its cost.
- **Owning chapter:** C02

<a id="gl-training-data"></a>

### training data

- **Definition:** The set of past examples a model learns from.
- **Example:** Millions of past payments with the outcome of whether each was later disputed.
- **Non-example:** The new cases the model will be used on.
- **Owning chapter:** C23

<a id="gl-trust-and-safety"></a>

### trust and safety

- **Definition:** The work of protecting users and a platform from abuse, fraud, harassment, harmful content and manipulation through policy, product design, detection and enforcement, against adversaries who adapt.
- **Example:** Designing layers of prevention, detection, review and appeals for a live-video feature.
- **Non-example:** A report button with no policy, detection or appeals behind it.
- **Owning chapter:** C27

<a id="gl-trust-signal"></a>

### trust signal

- **Definition:** A visible cue that tells a person a product, a person or a payment is legitimate and safe, whose absence can stop a transaction.
- **Example:** A cash agent who is a shopkeeper the customer already knows, or a receipt in the local language.
- **Non-example:** A security badge nobody recognizes.
- **Owning chapter:** C09

<a id="gl-two-sided-market"></a>

### two-sided market

- **Definition:** A market with two distinct groups of participants who need each other, where the platform's value to each group depends on the size and quality of the other.
- **Example:** Riders and drivers; buyers and sellers.
- **Non-example:** A product with many users who do not interact with one another.
- **Owning chapter:** C19

<a id="gl-underserved-user"></a>

### underserved user

- **Definition:** A person or group that existing products fail because of cost, access, ability or context, described by what the product lacks for them and not by who they are.
- **Example:** Adults in a rural district with a shared basic phone and no internet, who live far from a clinic.
- **Non-example:** "The poor," which is a label and gives no design direction.
- **Owning chapter:** C09

<a id="gl-unit-economics"></a>

### unit economics

- **Definition:** The revenue and cost attached to a single unit, such as a customer or an order, showing whether each unit makes money.
- **Example:** Average revenue per order minus delivery, payment and support cost per order.
- **Non-example:** Total company profit.
- **Owning chapter:** C18

<a id="gl-usability-heuristic"></a>

### usability heuristic

- **Definition:** A rule of thumb for judging whether an interface is easy to use, applied by an evaluator without users.
- **Example:** Checking that every error message says what went wrong and what to do next.
- **Non-example:** A usability test, which watches real users attempt tasks.
- **Owning chapter:** C10

<a id="gl-user-segment"></a>

### user segment

- **Definition:** A group of users defined by shared needs or behavior that matter to the decision at hand.
- **Example:** Weekly commuters who change routes often.
- **Non-example:** "Women", with no link to a need or behavior.
- **Owning chapter:** C06

<a id="gl-user-story"></a>

### user story

- **Definition:** A short description of a capability from the user's point of view, usually in the form 'As a [user], I want [capability] so that [benefit].'
- **Example:** As a shopper planning a trip with a friend, I want to share my packing list so that my friend can tick things off.
- **Non-example:** 'Add a share button,' which names a control and no purpose.
- **Owning chapter:** C16

<a id="gl-value-metric"></a>

### value metric

- **Definition:** The unit on which price is charged, such as seats, tasks, storage, transactions or outcomes, chosen so that price grows as the customer's value grows and as the seller's cost grows.
- **Example:** A per-seat price with an included allowance of tasks and a per-task overage.
- **Non-example:** A flat price unrelated to use.
- **Owning chapter:** C20

<a id="gl-vanity-metric"></a>

### vanity metric

- **Definition:** A number that rises reliably and flatters but does not tell you whether the product is working or what to do; a test is whether any decision would change if it fell.
- **Example:** Registered users, which only ever grows.
- **Non-example:** Weekly active users who return in each of four consecutive weeks, by cohort, with a guardrail.
- **Owning chapter:** C29

<a id="gl-webhook"></a>

### webhook

- **Definition:** A message one system sends to another's web address when an event happens, so the receiver need not keep asking.
- **Example:** A payments service telling a merchant's server that a payment succeeded.
- **Non-example:** A merchant polling every minute to ask whether anything changed.
- **Owning chapter:** C22

<a id="gl-willingness-to-pay"></a>

### willingness to pay

- **Definition:** The most a customer is prepared to pay for something, which varies by customer and by what they compare it with.
- **Example:** A survey in which 41% of target customers say they would buy at $449.
- **Non-example:** The cost of producing the product.
- **Owning chapter:** C20


<a id="appendix-a"></a>

# Appendix A. Google product briefs [as of 2026-10]

**What this is.** Eight one-page briefs on Google products, built with the method in C33.10 from public sources read in October 2026. They give you items 1 to 5 of the brief: the product and its users, how it fits the business, the metrics the company reports, where it stands, and recent moves. They deliberately leave out item 6 (your angle) and item 7 (your questions), because those must come from your own use of the product. Each brief ends with prompts to start from.

**These briefs are date-sensitive.** They describe products, fees, court cases, rules and figures as they stood in October 2026. Check each fact yourself at the time you read this book; the most perishable are the court schedules (A.1), the app store fees (A.6) and the payment shares and rules (A.8).

**How to use it.** Read a brief, then use the product for a week, then write your own angle. A brief that you recite is worth little in a loop. A brief that you test against your own use is worth a lot.

**Labels.** `Public` marks a statement from Google or Alphabet (a filing, a results release, a blog post by the company or its leaders). A figure marked "as reported" is one that the press attributes to a Google executive and that I did not find on a Google page. `Inferred` marks my reasoning, or what candidates and commentators say. Every figure carries the date it was checked. Check again before you rely on one (see the box "Dates to check" in C01).

<a id="app-a-a-0-the-business-in-one-table"></a>

## A.0 The business in one table

Alphabet's results for the quarter ended 30 June 2026 `Public` `[V: Alphabet Form 10-Q and results release, 2026]`:

| Line | Revenue, quarter ended 30 June 2026 | Change on the year |
|---|---|---|
| Google Search & other | $63.3 billion | up 17% |
| YouTube ads | $11.1 billion | up 13% |
| Google subscriptions, platforms and devices | $12.9 billion | up 15% |
| Google Cloud | $24.8 billion | up 82% |
| Alphabet in total | $119.8 billion | up 24% |

Search and other was a little over half of Alphabet's revenue that quarter (63.3 of 119.8, my arithmetic). The growth in subscriptions, platforms and devices came mainly from paid subscriptions across YouTube services and Google One, according to the 10-Q. The Gemini app had 950 million monthly active users, according to the results release.

<a id="app-a-a-1-google-search"></a>

## A.1 Google Search

**Product and users.** Search now offers AI Overviews and AI Mode as one experience. Google's CEO said on the Q2 2026 call that AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly active users after its global expansion in October 2025 `Public` `[V: Google, CEO remarks on the Q2 2026 call]`. AI Overviews was reported at more than 2 billion monthly users in July 2025 `Public` as reported `[V: trade press on the Q2 2025 call]`.

**How it fits.** Search is Alphabet's largest line (A.0). Alphabet reports its monetization as changes in paid clicks and cost per click, not as a price `[V: Alphabet 10-Q]`.

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** Google says AI features are adding queries and sending "billions of clicks to websites every week" `Public`. Publishers and independent researchers dispute how many clicks AI answers displace `Inferred` `[V: one 2026 statistics review; not tested here]`. Watch (`Inferred`): queries per user, the share of queries answered without a click, revenue per query, and latency.

**Where it stands.** A US court found in 2024 that Google held an illegal monopoly in search. In September 2025 the judge declined to order a sale of Chrome, required Google to share some search index and user-interaction data with rivals (not advertising data), and barred exclusive default deals `Public` `[V: court remedies order, as reported by Moneylife and The Desk]`. Google filed a notice of appeal in January 2026, and the Justice Department and states filed their own appeals by 3 February 2026 `[V: Bloomberg Law; a litigation tracker for Google's date]`. On 5 October 2026 the parties jointly asked the D.C. Circuit to give the cross-appeals priority so that oral argument could be held as early as 9 December `[V: Law360, 5 October 2026 (headline and summary)]` `[as of 2026-10]`. The judge wrote that generative AI had changed the course of the case `[V: reported by Folio3]`.

**Recent moves.** AI Overviews and AI Mode merged into one Search experience `Public` `[V: Google, CEO remarks on the Q2 2026 call]`. AI Mode had launched in the US and India by July 2025 `[V: trade press on the Q2 2025 call]`.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** If an AI answer satisfies the user, what should Search count as success? Who pays when the click disappears? What would you ask legal and policy before you changed a default?

<a id="app-a-a-2-google-maps"></a>

## A.2 Google Maps

**Product and users.** More than 2 billion people use Maps `Public` `[V: Associated Press report of Google's 12 March 2026 announcement]`.

**How it fits.** I found no separate Maps revenue figure in the filings or reports I read. Treat its business role as an open question to answer from your own reading (`Inferred`).

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** On 12 March 2026 Google announced two Gemini features. Ask Maps lets people ask questions in plain language and draws on information from more than 300 million places, including community reviews `[V: as reported from Google's blog post]`. It rolled out in the US and India first. Immersive Navigation is a 3D redesign of driving directions that Google called its biggest navigation upgrade in over a decade, starting in the US `[V: AP; Noqta summary of the blog post]`. Watch (`Inferred`): navigation sessions completed, place-search success, and trust in recommendations.

**Where it stands and recent moves.** The AP report says Google believes its safeguards stop Gemini from inventing places `[V: AP]`. That claim is Google's, and it is the claim to test.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** What does a wrong answer cost in a map compared with a chat? Which users would you roll Ask Maps out to first, and why India second?

<a id="app-a-a-3-youtube"></a>

## A.3 YouTube

**Product and users.** YouTube ads earned $11.1 billion in the quarter ended 30 June 2026, up 13% `Public` `[V: Alphabet Form 10-Q]`. Over 1.7 billion unique viewers watched World Cup videos on YouTube during the 2026 tournament `Public` `[V: Alphabet results release]`.

**How it fits.** Two revenue streams: ads (A.0) and subscriptions, which Alphabet reports inside subscriptions, platforms and devices.

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** As reported: YouTube's revenue across ads and subscriptions passed $60 billion in 2025 `[V: Alphabet Q4 2025 call, as relayed by a statistics roundup]`. YouTube Music and Premium had over 125 million subscribers, and paid subscriptions across YouTube and Google One reached 350 million by the first quarter of 2026 `[V: CEO statements as relayed by TIKR from MoffettNathanson and Alphabet's Q1 2026 release]`. Shorts is reported at about 200 billion daily views, and one source notes that the counting rules changed during the run `[V: a 2026 statistics review]`. I did not open YouTube's own pages for these figures. Watch (`Inferred`): watch time on TV screens against mobile, Shorts revenue per hour, creator payouts.

**Where it stands.** YouTube's CEO said it paid more than $100 billion to creators, artists and media companies over four years `[V: as reported]`.

**Recent moves.** Cheaper and genre-specific plans (a Premium Lite and genre plans for YouTube TV) were reported in May 2026 `[V: TIKR]`.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** If Shorts earns the same per hour as long video, what changes in recommendations? How would you tell a subscriber you won from one you merely moved?

<a id="app-a-a-4-gmail"></a>

## A.4 Gmail

**Product and users.** About 3 billion people use Gmail `Public` `[V: Google, "Gmail is entering the Gemini era," 8 January 2026]`.

**How it fits.** Gmail is a reach product that anchors Google accounts, storage and subscriptions `Inferred`. Alphabet's filings I read do not break out Gmail revenue.

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** On 8 January 2026 Google released Help Me Write and Suggested Replies to everyone at no cost; Proofread and "ask your inbox" answers went to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers; and AI Inbox was a test with trusted testers `Public` `[V: Google blog]`. Google's data, as reported by Fortune, was that 70% of enterprise users of Help Me Write in Docs or Gmail accepted the suggestion `[V: Fortune]`. Watch (`Inferred`): acceptance of suggestions, edits after acceptance, and opt-out of smart features.

**Where it stands and recent moves.** The features began in US English only `[V: Google; Fortune]`. Which features are free and which are paid is a live packaging decision.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** What would "the inbox is better" mean as a number? Which Gemini feature would you keep free and which paid, and what evidence would you want?

<a id="app-a-a-5-google-photos"></a>

## A.5 Google Photos

**Product and users.** More than 1.5 billion monthly users and more than 9 trillion photos and videos stored, per Google's 10th-anniversary figures of May 2025 `Public` as reported `[V: Ars Technica, 28 May 2025]`. Users run over 370 million searches in Photos each month, as reported by the same source.

**How it fits.** Storage and editing drive paid plans. Since 2021, uploads count against the 15 GB that every Google Account shares across Photos, Gmail and Drive, and Google encourages paid Google One storage `[V: Ars Technica]`. Alphabet says growth in Google One subscriptions drives part of its subscriptions line `[V: Alphabet 10-Q]`.

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** The Create tab holds the AI features: Remix and photo-to-video launched in July 2025 as experiments that ask for a thumbs-up or down `[V: TechCrunch, 23 July 2025]`. A Video Remix feature began rolling out to Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers in July 2026 `[V: Thurrott]`. Watch (`Inferred`): photos edited, searches, storage-plan upgrades, and thumbs-down rate on generated media.

**Where it stands.** Photos began in 2015 as a spin-out from Google+ `[V: Ars Technica]`.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** What is the product's job: memory, backup or creation? Which metric would tell you a free user is about to pay for storage?

<a id="app-a-a-6-android-and-google-play"></a>

## A.6 Android and Google Play

**Product and users.** Android is the operating system, and Google Play is its main app store.

**How it fits.** Play sits in the subscriptions, platforms and devices line (A.0). Google's standard service fee has been 15% on a developer's first $1 million and 30% beyond `[V: Android Authority]`.

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** Google's Play policy page says the US injunction in the Epic Games case was upheld by the Ninth Circuit on 12 September 2025, and lists compliance steps: developers may link users to outside offers from 29 October 2025, Play began sharing its catalog with third-party US app stores in July 2026, and developers in the alternative-billing programs must report transactions and pay fees from 1 October 2026 `Public` `[V: Google Play Console policy page]`. Rival app stores can be installed from Play in the US from 22 July 2026, with a $5,000 annual review fee for stores `[V: PocketGamer.biz]`. Watch (`Inferred`): the share of installs outside Play, developer retention, and security incidents from alternative stores.

**Where it stands and recent moves.** Google and Epic announced a settlement in March 2026 with lower fees and a registered-app-store program outside the US, then withdrew their joint motion in July 2026 to change the injunction `[V: TechCrunch; PocketGamer.biz]`. Reports say Google began separating service fees from billing fees on 30 June 2026 and will require developer identity verification in four countries from September 2026 `[V: PocketGamer.biz news index]`. The fee structure announced in June 2026 charges a 10% service fee on the first $1 million a year, then 20% for new installs or 25% for existing installs above that, with link-out fees of 20% above $1 million and an extra 5% when a developer uses Google's billing system; it applies in the UK, the EEA and the US first, in Australia, Japan and South Korea by the end of 2026, and elsewhere by September 2027 `[V: MacRumors, 24 June 2026; Help Net Security, 5 March 2026 (the settlement terms)]` `[as of 2026-10]`.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** What do you protect about security when anyone can run a store? How would you price Play if every fee could be avoided?

<a id="app-a-a-7-gemini"></a>

## A.7 Gemini

**Product and users.** The Gemini app had 950 million monthly active users and daily users tripled in the past year, and Gemini models processed about 22 billion API tokens a minute `Public` `[V: Alphabet results release and the CEO's Q2 2026 remarks]`.

**How it fits.** Gemini is both a product and the engine inside others. Gemini 3 powered the Gmail features in January 2026 `[V: Google blog]`, and a model called Gemini Omni was reported behind Video Remix in Photos and free AI video in YouTube Shorts `[V: Thurrott; Ngram, as reported]`. Paid tiers are Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra `[V: Thurrott]`.

**What Google reports, and what to watch.** Alphabet reports usage (monthly users, tokens) and Cloud revenue, which grew 82% to $24.8 billion with a backlog of $514 billion `Public` `[V: Alphabet results; CEO remarks]`. Watch (`Inferred`): retention of monthly users, answer quality on your own tasks, and what the free tier gives away.

**Where it stands.** Coverage names ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude as rivals for the kind of questions people once typed into Search `[V: a 2026 article on the search appeal]`, which is why the Search and Gemini briefs belong together.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** If Gemini answers what Search used to answer, which product owns the user? How would you decide what a Gemini feature must not do?

<a id="app-a-a-8-google-pay-in-india"></a>

## A.8 Google Pay in India

**Product and users.** A UPI app that lets people pay from a bank account. UPI was piloted on 11 April 2016 with 21 banks, and the apps came to Google Play from 25 August 2016 `Public` `[V: NPCI product overview and press release]`.

**How it fits.** UPI apps may not charge consumers a platform fee `Public` `[V: UPI merchant-fee FAQs dated 15 September 2026]`, so an app's value is indirect: usage, trust and the user relationship `Inferred`. From 15 October 2026 a 0.4% merchant fee applies to person-to-merchant payments above ₹2,000, shared within the UPI ecosystem (see C09).

**What the numbers say.** PhonePe and Google Pay together handled about 79% of UPI payments in May 2026, below 80% for the first time, with PhonePe near 46% `[V: NPCI data as reported by Outlook Business and Adda247]`. For July 2026 the two held 78.6%, with PhonePe near 46% `[V: NPCI data as reported by StartupFeed]` `[as of 2026-10]`. In November 2024, Reuters reported PhonePe at 47.8% and Google Pay at 37%.

**Where it stands.** NPCI's rule caps any one third-party app at 30% of UPI volume. The deadline was extended twice and now falls on 31 December 2026 `Public` `[V: NPCI statement as reported by Business Today and MediaNama]`. Reports say Google Pay and PhonePe both exceed 30%, and that an app above the cap would have to stop onboarding new customers `[V: Inc42; MediaNama]`.

**Recent moves.** The merchant-fee framework (15 October 2026) and the NPCI cap (31 December 2026) both change what an app can earn and how it can grow `Inferred`.

**Prompts (`Inferred`).** If you could not onboard new users past the cap, where would growth come from? What product would earn money when the payment itself is free?


<a id="appendix-b"></a>

# Appendix B. Practice data and SQL scripts [as of 2026-10]

**What this is.** The SQL in C13.6a, in the worked examples and exercises of C13, and in the practice plan of C37 runs on small invented datasets. This appendix gives the three short scripts that build them and the queries the chapters quote, so you can run every one and see the numbers the chapters report. All data are invented; none describes a real product or user.

**How to run.** Save each script in a file with the name in its first line and run it with Python 3, which includes SQLite and needs nothing else. Date and string functions differ between databases, so check your own dialect before copying a query to another system. Each script prints its results; the numbers quoted in the chapters were checked against them.

**Which chapter uses which script.**

| Script | Dataset | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5,000 users and their events over three weeks, with three acquisition channels (seed 42) | C13.6a and its worked examples and exercises; the analytics practice in C37 |
| 2 | Three weekly cohorts of 2,000 signups whose channel mix shifts while each channel's rate stays fixed (seed 11) | C13.6a, the mix-shift example |
| 3 | A "test table" of 10,000 visits, 2,400 add-to-carts and 600 purchases, with 300 repeat add-to-carts | The funnel-count exercise in C13 |

<a id="app-b-b-1-script-1-the-practice-dataset-and-its-queries"></a>

## B.1 Script 1: the practice dataset and its queries

Key results to expect: the funnel returns 5,000 signed up, 2,574 activated and 530 purchased; activation by channel is 53.7% (organic, 2,248 signups), 40.1% (paid, 1,745) and 66.2% (referral, 1,007); the fan-out query returns 7,574 rows for 5,000 users; the two definitions of week-1 return give 107 and 745.

```python
# Script 1: the practice dataset (5,000 invented users) and the queries run on it in C13 and C37.
# Run: python3 practice_data.py   (creates sandbox.db in the current folder; needs only Python, which includes SQLite).
import sqlite3, random, datetime as dt
random.seed(42)
con=sqlite3.connect('sandbox.db'); c=con.cursor()
c.executescript("""
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS events;
CREATE TABLE users(user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, signup_date TEXT, channel TEXT);
CREATE TABLE events(user_id INTEGER, event TEXT, event_date TEXT);
""")
start=dt.date(2027,1,4)  # a Monday
channels=[('organic',.45,.55,.30),('paid',.35,.40,.20),('referral',.20,.65,.35)]  # name, share, p_activate, p_week1_return|activated
uid=0
for i in range(5000):
    uid+=1
    d=start+dt.timedelta(days=random.randint(0,20))
    r=random.random(); acc=0
    for name,sh,pa,pr in channels:
        acc+=sh
        if r<=acc: ch=name; pact=pa; pret=pr; break
    c.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES(?,?,?)",(uid,d.isoformat(),ch))
    c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)",(uid,'signup',d.isoformat()))
    if random.random()<pact:
        ad=d+dt.timedelta(days=random.randint(0,2))
        c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)",(uid,'activated',ad.isoformat()))
        if random.random()<pret:
            rd=d+dt.timedelta(days=random.randint(7,13))
            c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)",(uid,'returned',rd.isoformat()))
        if random.random()<0.22:
            pd=d+dt.timedelta(days=random.randint(1,10))
            c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)",(uid,'purchased',pd.isoformat()))
con.commit()

QUERIES = [
    ("C13.6a, a funnel in one pass", """
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event='signup'    THEN user_id END) AS signed_up,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event='activated' THEN user_id END) AS activated,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event='purchased' THEN user_id END) AS purchased
FROM events;
"""),
    ("C13.6a, a rate by segment", """
SELECT u.channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS signups,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS activated,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS activation_pct
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN events a ON a.user_id = u.user_id AND a.event = 'activated'
GROUP BY u.channel;
"""),
    ("C13.6a, a cohort by signup week", """
SELECT strftime('%Y-%W', u.signup_date) AS signup_week,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS signups,
       COUNT(DISTINCT r.user_id) AS returned,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT r.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS return_pct
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN events r ON r.user_id = u.user_id AND r.event = 'returned'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
"""),
    ("C13 worked query, daily active users (first six days shown)", """
SELECT event_date, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
FROM events
WHERE event IN ('signup', 'activated')   -- whichever events define "active"
GROUP BY event_date
ORDER BY event_date;
"""),
    ("C13 worked query, two definitions of week-1 return (107 and 745)", """
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN CAST(julianday(r.event_date) - julianday(u.signup_date) AS INT) BETWEEN 1 AND 7
                           THEN u.user_id END) AS returned_days_1_to_7,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN CAST(julianday(r.event_date) - julianday(u.signup_date) AS INT) BETWEEN 7 AND 13
                           THEN u.user_id END) AS returned_days_7_to_13
FROM users u
JOIN events r ON r.user_id = u.user_id AND r.event = 'returned';
"""),
    ("C13 worked query, return rate by channel and signup week", """
WITH base AS (
  SELECT u.user_id,
         strftime('%Y-%W', u.signup_date) AS signup_week,
         u.channel,
         MAX(CASE WHEN e.event = 'returned'
                   AND CAST(julianday(e.event_date) - julianday(u.signup_date) AS INT) BETWEEN 7 AND 13
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned
  FROM users u
  LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.user_id
  GROUP BY u.user_id)
SELECT signup_week, channel, COUNT(*) AS signups, SUM(returned) AS returned,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(returned) / COUNT(*), 1) AS return_pct
FROM base GROUP BY signup_week, channel ORDER BY signup_week, channel;
"""),
    ("Failure: fan-out (7,574 rows for 5,000 users)", """
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM users u JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.user_id AND e.event IN ('signup', 'activated');
"""),
    ("Failure: an inner join removes the denominator (1,208 of 1,208 for organic)", """
SELECT u.channel, COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id)
FROM users u JOIN events a ON a.user_id = u.user_id AND a.event = 'activated'
GROUP BY u.channel;
"""),
]
for title, q in QUERIES:
    print('\n##', title)
    for i, row in enumerate(c.execute(q)):
        if i == 6: print('...'); break
        print(row)
```

<a id="app-b-b-2-script-2-a-mix-shift"></a>

## B.2 Script 2: a mix shift

Key results to expect: overall activation falls from 53.95% to 51.10% to 47.50% by signup week, while each channel's own rate stays about the same; the decomposition from week 1 to week 3 gives a rate effect of −1.41 points and a mix effect of −5.04 points, a total of −6.45 points.

```python
# Script 2: a synthetic dataset for C13.6a in which overall activation falls week over week while every channel's rate stays the same (seed 11).
# Run: python3 mixshift.py
import sqlite3, random, datetime as dt
random.seed(11)
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); c = con.cursor()
c.executescript("CREATE TABLE users(user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, signup_date TEXT, channel TEXT, activated INTEGER);")
rate = {"organic": .54, "paid": .40, "referral": .66}
mix = {1: [("organic", .50), ("paid", .20), ("referral", .30)],
       2: [("organic", .45), ("paid", .35), ("referral", .20)],
       3: [("organic", .35), ("paid", .50), ("referral", .15)]}
start = dt.date(2027, 3, 1); uid = 0
for w in (1, 2, 3):
    for _ in range(2000):
        uid += 1; r = random.random(); acc = 0
        for ch, sh in mix[w]:
            acc += sh
            if r <= acc: break
        d = start + dt.timedelta(days=7 * (w - 1) + random.randint(0, 6))
        c.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES(?,?,?,?)", (uid, d.isoformat(), ch, 1 if random.random() < rate[ch] else 0))
def run(title, q):
    print("\n##", title)
    for r in c.execute(q): print(r)
base = "CAST((julianday(signup_date)-julianday('2027-03-01'))/7 AS INT)+1"
run("Q1 overall activation by signup week", f"""SELECT {base} AS wk, COUNT(*) AS signups, SUM(activated) AS activated,
 ROUND(100.0*SUM(activated)/COUNT(*),2) AS activation_pct FROM users GROUP BY wk ORDER BY wk""")
run("Q2 by week and channel: share of signups and activation rate", f"""WITH t AS (SELECT {base} AS wk, channel, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(activated) AS a FROM users GROUP BY wk, channel),
 w AS (SELECT wk, SUM(n) AS total FROM t GROUP BY wk)
SELECT t.wk, t.channel, t.n, ROUND(100.0*t.n/w.total,1) AS share_pct, ROUND(100.0*t.a/t.n,1) AS rate_pct
FROM t JOIN w USING(wk) ORDER BY t.wk, t.channel""")
run("Q3 decomposition week 1 to week 3 (rate effect at old shares, mix effect at new rates, percentage points)", f"""WITH t AS (SELECT {base} AS wk, channel, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(activated) AS a FROM users GROUP BY wk, channel),
 w AS (SELECT wk, SUM(n) AS total FROM t GROUP BY wk),
 s AS (SELECT t.wk, t.channel, 1.0*t.n/w.total AS share, 1.0*t.a/t.n AS rate FROM t JOIN w USING(wk)),
 x AS (SELECT s1.channel, s1.share AS sh1, s1.rate AS r1, s3.share AS sh3, s3.rate AS r3 FROM s s1 JOIN s s3 ON s1.channel=s3.channel AND s1.wk=1 AND s3.wk=3)
SELECT ROUND(100*SUM(sh1*(r3-r1)),2) AS rate_effect_pp, ROUND(100*SUM((sh3-sh1)*r3),2) AS mix_effect_pp,
 ROUND(100*SUM(sh3*r3)-100*SUM(sh1*r1),2) AS total_change_pp FROM x""")
run("Q4 mix-adjusted activation at the week-1 mix", f"""WITH t AS (SELECT {base} AS wk, channel, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(activated) AS a FROM users GROUP BY wk, channel),
 w AS (SELECT wk, SUM(n) AS total FROM t GROUP BY wk),
 s AS (SELECT t.wk, t.channel, 1.0*t.n/w.total AS share, 1.0*t.a/t.n AS rate FROM t JOIN w USING(wk))
SELECT ROUND(100*SUM(s1.share*s3.rate),2) AS week3_rates_at_week1_mix FROM s s1 JOIN s s3 ON s1.channel=s3.channel AND s1.wk=1 AND s3.wk=3""")
```

## B.3 Script 3: the funnel-count exercise

Key results to expect: 10,000 users visited, 2,400 added to cart and 600 purchased; counting `add_to_cart` rows instead of users gives 2,700.

```python
# Script 3: the "test table" of the exercise on funnel counts in C13 (invented): 10,000 users visited, 2,400 added to cart,
# 600 purchased, and 300 of the users who added to cart did so on two different days.
# Run: python3 test_table.py
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); c = con.cursor()
c.execute("CREATE TABLE events(user_id INTEGER, event TEXT, event_date TEXT)")
for u in range(1, 10001): c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)", (u, "visit", "2027-02-01"))
for u in range(1, 2401): c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)", (u, "add_to_cart", "2027-02-01"))
for u in range(1, 301): c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)", (u, "add_to_cart", "2027-02-02"))
for u in range(1, 601): c.execute("INSERT INTO events VALUES(?,?,?)", (u, "purchase", "2027-02-02"))
print("users per step:", c.execute("""SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event='visit' THEN user_id END),
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event='add_to_cart' THEN user_id END),
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event='purchase' THEN user_id END) FROM events""").fetchone())
print("add_to_cart rows (the wrong count):", c.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event='add_to_cart'").fetchone()[0])
```

<a id="appendix-c"></a>

# Appendix C. Competency matrix

The ten competencies that interview loops probe, the three bands used by every chapter's rubric (Baseline, Strong, Standout), the weight each carries in interviews, and where the book teaches it. It is the scoring rubric behind the self-assessment in C01 and the mock-interview scorecards in C34. Company differences are in the company lens of each chapter and in C33.

<a id="app-c-c-0-how-to-read-this-document"></a>

## C.0 How to read this document

**Bands** (used by every chapter rubric and by Appendix E):

| Band | Meaning | What an interviewer would write |
|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Passes a screen on this dimension. Unlikely to clear a hiring decision by itself. | "Knew the vocabulary; answer was generic or unstructured." |
| **Strong** | Clear hire signal on this dimension. | "Structured, made explicit choices, justified them." |
| **Standout** | Top of the pool. The dimension is a reason to hire. | "Changed how I think about the problem; would want on my team." |

**Provenance of the bands.** Companies do not publish scoring rubrics at this resolution. The behaviors below are an **Original** synthesis, built from public hiring attributes (C.1) and from the structure of the questions commonly reported by candidates and prep sources. Where a claim is about what a specific company does, it carries `Public` or `Inferred`. Time-sensitive claims carry `[as of 2026-10, verify]`.

---

<a id="app-c-c-1-company-signal-map-calibration-only-not-a-rubric"></a>

## C.1 Company signal map (calibration only, not a rubric)

I checked public material on the Google APM process. Results were third-party prep sites and a university career-center page, **not Google itself**, so process details are `Inferred` and may be stale.

| Company | Public signals | Reported format | Label |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Google (APM)** | Google publicly describes hiring on four attributes: general cognitive ability, role-related knowledge, leadership, and "Googleyness." | Two-year rotational program per prep sources. Reported loop: phone screen, then several rounds across product sense, execution/analytical, behavioral and estimation, then committee review and often a final conversation. Reported acceptance rate is very low in some years, source unclear. | Attributes: `Public` `[verify]`. Format: `Inferred` `[as of 2026-10, verify]` |
| **Meta (RPM)** | Rotational PM program referenced by prep sources. | Commonly described as product sense, execution (analytical) and leadership rounds. | `Inferred` `[as of 2026-10, verify]` |
| **Amazon** | Amazon publishes its Leadership Principles and ties interviews to them. | Behavioral questions mapped to principles, plus product and technical depth. Entry routes include technical PM roles `[verify]`. | Principles: `Public`. Routes and format: `Inferred` `[verify]` |
| **Microsoft** | Publicly emphasizes a growth-mindset culture. | Early-career PM entry points and loop format vary by org. | Culture: `Public`. Format: `Inferred` `[verify]` |
| **Apple, Netflix** | No formal rotational APM program known to me. | Entry usually via other roles or experienced hiring. | `Inferred` `[verify]` |
| **Stripe, Atlassian, Uber, others** | Stripe and Atlassian reported to run APM-style programs. | Varies. | `Inferred` `[verify]` |

**Implication for design:** the competency set below is the intersection that every one of these loops probes under different names. Company differences go in per-chapter **Company lens** sections, not in separate chapters.

---

<a id="app-c-c-2-the-ten-competencies"></a>

## C.2 The ten competencies

Interview weight is `Inferred` from the reported round structure (C.1): **High** = a dedicated round at most companies; **Med** = embedded in rounds; **Low** = occasional.

<a id="app-c-c-2-1-product-sense-product-sense-tier-1-weight-high"></a>

### C.2.1 Product sense (`product-sense`) — Tier 1 — weight: **High**

*Includes:* designing for a user, improving an existing product, designing for a new market, critiquing a product.
*Scored in:* dedicated product sense/design round (`Inferred`); on the job: choosing what to build for whom.

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Restates the prompt. Picks a user group by demographics ("college students"). Lists features. Offers one solution. Names a metric without linking it to the goal. |
| **Strong** | Clarifies product, goal and constraints in under two minutes. Segments users by need or behavior and picks one with a stated criterion. Ranks pain points by frequency and severity. Offers three solutions that differ in kind, not in degree. Compares them on impact, effort and risk, recommends one, and defines a success metric with a guardrail. |
| **Standout** | Reframes the problem around the underlying job, not the surface request. Ties the choice to the company's actual advantage. Surfaces a non-obvious user or insight and says why it is non-obvious. Kills one of their own ideas on stated grounds. Names second-order effects (abuse, trust, ecosystem, cannibalization). Adjusts live when the interviewer pushes back, without abandoning the structure. Closes with a phased plan and what evidence would change the decision. |

*Failure signature:* feature list with no user; solution fixed before the problem is defined; "make it better" metrics.

<a id="app-c-c-2-2-user-research-and-discovery-discovery-tier-1-weight-me"></a>

### C.2.2 User research and discovery (`discovery`) — Tier 1 — weight: **Med**

*Scored in:* product sense round (user understanding), behavioral round ("how did you learn what users needed?"), occasionally a "plan the research" prompt (`Inferred`).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | "Run surveys and interviews." Treats what users say as what they need. |
| **Strong** | Separates problem, solution and feature. Picks method to fit the question (qual to find, quant to size). Writes non-leading questions. Names sampling and bias risks. Turns findings into a problem statement a team could act on. |
| **Standout** | Designs the cheapest test that could falsify the riskiest assumption. Contrasts stated versus observed behavior and explains the gap. States what the research cannot tell you. Shows a real decision that changed because of evidence, from their own work. |

*Failure signature:* asking users to design the product; research as ritual with no decision attached.

<a id="app-c-c-2-3-problem-solving-problem-solving-tier-1-weight-high"></a>

### C.2.3 Problem solving (`problem-solving`) — Tier 1 — weight: **High**

*Sub-skills:* structuring (MECE, issue trees, hypotheses), root-cause analysis, estimation.
*Scored in:* analytical rounds, estimation rounds (reported as program-specific at Google, `Inferred`), and implicitly in every round.

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Recites a named framework. Categories overlap or omit something obvious. Estimate has numbers but no stated assumptions; no sanity check. |
| **Strong** | Clarifies the question before structuring. Builds a tree cut along the dimension that matters for the decision, with non-overlapping, exhaustive branches. Prioritizes branches by likelihood and cost to check. States each estimation assumption aloud, uses round numbers, cross-checks with a second route. |
| **Standout** | Works hypothesis-first and says which branch they would test first and why. Chooses the cut because of the decision it supports. Quantifies which branch matters most. Reports estimates as ranges and says what would move them. Ends estimation with "so what": what decision this number changes. Recovers visibly when an assumption is challenged. |

*Failure signature:* framework theater (naming a framework instead of using it); overlapping branches; precision without a sanity check.

<a id="app-c-c-2-4-analytics-and-experimentation-analytics-tier-1-weight-"></a>

### C.2.4 Analytics and experimentation (`analytics`) — Tier 1 — weight: **High**

*Includes:* choosing metrics, funnels and cohorts, diagnosing a metric change, experiment design, causal reasoning.
*Scored in:* analytical/execution round (`Inferred`); on the job: reading dashboards and experiment readouts.

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Names DAU/MAU and "look at the funnel." Knows A/B tests exist. For a metric drop, jumps to a favorite cause. |
| **Strong** | Defines a north star with input metrics and guardrails; states each metric precisely (numerator, denominator, window, population). Diagnoses in a fixed order: check the data, then segment (time, platform, geography, cohort, funnel step), then separate internal from external causes, then form causal hypotheses. Designs an experiment: unit, randomization, duration, primary and guardrail metrics, decision rule. |
| **Standout** | Reasons causally: confounders, selection effects, sample-ratio mismatch, novelty effects, interference between users, Simpson's paradox. Chooses a fallback when a randomized test is impossible and states its weakness. Anticipates how a metric will be gamed. Balances short- and long-term effects. States the threshold at which they would ship, hold or roll back, before seeing results. |

*Failure signature:* metric lists without definitions; "run an A/B test" as the answer to everything; confusing correlation with the cause of a drop.

<a id="app-c-c-2-5-execution-execution-tier-1-weight-high"></a>

### C.2.5 Execution (`execution`) — Tier 1 — weight: **High**

*Includes:* prioritization, tradeoffs, PRDs, launch decisions, working with engineering and design.
*Scored in:* execution round and behavioral round (`Inferred`).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Lists steps. Cites RICE or MoSCoW by name; ranks by gut. |
| **Strong** | States the objective and what "done" means. Scopes an MVP and says what was cut and why. Prioritizes with explicit criteria. Sequences work by dependency. Names risks with mitigations. Defines rollout stages, success criteria and a rollback trigger. |
| **Standout** | Decides under constraint with options: "cut scope, move date, or add capacity; I recommend X because Y." Separates reversible from irreversible decisions. Instruments before launch. Sets kill criteria in advance. Handles "engineering says 3x longer" and "launch metric regressed" with a concrete decision path and the stakeholder communication to go with it. |

*Failure signature:* plan without tradeoffs; every item "P0"; no decision rule for launch.

<a id="app-c-c-2-6-technical-fluency-technical-tier-1-weight-med-high-for"></a>

### C.2.6 Technical fluency (`technical`) — Tier 1 — weight: **Med** (High for technical-leaning roles)

*Includes:* how products work, APIs, data, PM-level system design.
*Scored in:* technical/system round where present, and implicitly via credibility with engineers (`Inferred`).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Uses terms (API, database, cloud) loosely. Cannot trace a user action through the system. |
| **Strong** | Walks a request end to end (client, network, service, data store, response). Explains APIs and data models at box-and-arrow level. Names latency, scale and reliability tradeoffs and what each costs the user. Covers privacy and security basics. Asks engineer-grade clarifying questions. |
| **Standout** | Ties each technical choice to a user outcome and a cost. Finds the bottleneck and the likely failure mode. Gives order-of-magnitude capacity estimates. Frames build versus buy and tech-debt decisions as product decisions. Explains the same design to an engineer and to an executive at two levels. |

*Failure signature:* buzzword fluency; designing a system with no product requirements; hiding behind "that's an engineering question."

<a id="app-c-c-2-7-ai-product-thinking-ai-tier-1-weight-med-and-rising-in"></a>

### C.2.7 AI product thinking (`ai`) — Tier 1 — weight: **Med and rising** `Inferred`

*Includes:* LLM products, RAG, agents, evals, safety, cost and latency.
*Scored in:* AI-specific product questions where offered, and in any product design question where AI is the obvious tool (`Inferred`).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | "Add an LLM." Knows hallucination exists. No view on cost or failure. |
| **Strong** | Decides whether AI is the right tool, and says why or why not. Defines the task, the data and the cost of a wrong answer. Proposes evals (offline set, online metrics). Names the quality, cost and latency tradeoff. Designs fallbacks and human review. Distinguishes prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning. |
| **Standout** | Writes the eval before the feature. Designs a trust progression for autonomy. Works out unit economics at scale. Handles non-determinism in the UX. Names privacy, safety and compliance risks specific to the use case. States what is likely to change with better models and what will not. |

*Failure signature:* AI as decoration; demo-quality thinking with no eval; ignoring per-query cost.

<a id="app-c-c-2-8-design-and-ux-design-ux-tier-2-weight-med"></a>

### C.2.8 Design and UX (`design-ux`) — Tier 2 — weight: **Med**

*Scored in:* product sense round (flows, critique) and execution (working with design) (`Inferred`).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Recites heuristics. "Make it simpler." |
| **Strong** | Critiques an interface against the user's goal, in priority order. Sketches a flow, including empty, error and loading states. Weighs speed against craft. Covers accessibility basics. |
| **Standout** | Ties each design issue to a metric or a user outcome. Designs for edge users (low bandwidth, low literacy, assistive tech). Spots dark patterns and declines them with a reason. Knows when the problem is not a design problem. |

*Failure signature:* critique by taste ("I don't like it"); redesigning without a user.

<a id="app-c-c-2-9-strategy-and-gtm-at-apm-depth-strategy-gtm-tier-1-stra"></a>

### C.2.9 Strategy and GTM at APM depth (`strategy-gtm`) — Tier 1 (strategy) / Tier 2 (GTM, pricing, growth) — weight: **Med**

*Scored in:* strategy/business round where present, otherwise within product sense (`Inferred`). No P&L ownership expected at this level.

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Lists competitors; fills a SWOT. |
| **Strong** | Answers "should X enter Y?" with criteria: market attractiveness, right to win, economics, risk. States a thesis and a recommendation with conditions. Explains positioning, a pricing model and distribution choices. |
| **Standout** | Identifies the source of advantage (distribution, data, switching costs, network effects). Anticipates competitor response. Sequences from a wedge to expansion. Sanity-checks unit economics. States what would prove the thesis wrong. For launches, names channel, message and the first 1,000 users. |

*Failure signature:* generic market description; strategy without a choice; ignoring incumbents' reaction.

<a id="app-c-c-2-10-behavioral-and-communication-behavioral-tier-1-weight"></a>

### C.2.10 Behavioral and communication (`behavioral`) — Tier 1 — weight: **High as a gate**

*Scored in:* behavioral/leadership round, and in how every other answer is delivered (`Inferred`). Amazon makes the link to published principles explicit (`Public`).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Stories lack specifics. "We" throughout; the candidate's role is unclear. No outcome, no learning. |
| **Strong** | Each story states context, the decision they personally made, the action, the measurable result and what they would change. Answers the question asked. Under two minutes unless probed. Has stories for conflict, failure, influence without authority, ambiguity and customer focus. |
| **Standout** | Holds up under three levels of follow-up questions. Failure story shows a changed behavior, not just a lesson. Disagreement story shows respect for the other side and a real cost to the candidate. Maps stories to the company's stated attributes without sounding scripted. Adjusts length and depth to interviewer cues. |

*Failure signature:* rehearsed monologue; hero narrative with no cost; vagueness about personal contribution.

---

<a id="app-c-c-3-cross-cutting-layer-interview-craft-interview-craft-tier"></a>

## C.3 Cross-cutting layer: interview craft (`interview-craft`) — Tier 1

Not a scored competency, but it multiplies all ten. It is a Tier 1 topic in this book (loop structure, company-specific formats, mock system).

| Band | Observable behaviors |
|---|---|
| **Baseline** | Starts answering immediately. No signposting. Runs out of time before recommending. |
| **Strong** | Clarifies, then states the plan ("I'll cover users, problems, solutions, metrics"). Signposts. Spends the first third on definition and the last third on decision and metrics. Closes with a one-sentence recommendation. |
| **Standout** | Reads interviewer cues and reallocates time. Invites steering. Treats pushback as data. Keeps a visible thread from problem to metric. Stays calm when stuck and says how they would unstick themselves. |

---
